cases.answerText: For a manifold serving 30 tons of refrigeration, the minimum condensate pipe diameter is **1 inch** under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code. The table places 30 tons in the “Over 20 tons to 40 tons” range; the table specifies diameter, while the section’s separate baseline is at least 3/4-inch internal diameter for condensate drain lines. (MC § 307.2.2)

cases.label: correct_useful

cases.answerText: At exactly **20 tons of refrigeration**, the applicable table row is “Up to 20 tons,” so the minimum diameter for a manifold serving more than one unit is **3/4 inch**—not the 1-inch minimum for capacity over 20 through 40 tons. Condensate drain lines also must be at least 3/4-inch internal diameter and cannot decrease in size from the drain-pan connection to disposal. (PC § 314.2.2)

Condensate drain lines must also be at least ¾-inch internal diameter and cannot decrease in size from the drain-pan connection to disposal. (PC § 314.2.2)

The table row “Over 125 tons to 250 tons of refrigeration” includes 200 tons. The line must also be at least 3/4-inch internal diameter and must not decrease in size from the drain-pan connection to disposal (PC § 314.2.2).

cases.answerText: No. Under 2022 NYC FGC § 409.5.1, the shutoff must be in the same room **and within 6 feet of the appliance**; 8 feet exceeds that limit. The section’s stated exception concerns only a valve located more than 60 inches above the finished floor, not the 6-foot distance. You stipulated that no other exception applies.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Gas-valve distance, room and height exception correctly applied to changing scenario.
cases.answerText: Yes. Exactly 6 feet meets the 2022 NYC FGC limit of “within 6 feet” of the appliance. That answers the distance requirement alone; the valve must also be in the same room, upstream of the union, connector, or quick-disconnect it serves, accessible, and no more than 60 inches above the finished floor. The stated height exception does not change the 6-foot limit. (FGC § 409.5.1)

cases.label: correct_useful

cases.answerText: **No.** At 4 feet, the valve meets the distance limit, but a different room does not meet the separate same-room requirement (2022 NYC FGC § 409.5.1). A specific rule permits remote valves for vented decorative appliances and room heaters if they are readily accessible, permanently identified, serve no other appliance, and the piping conditions are met (§ 409.5.2); on your stated premise that no exception applies, that allowance does not change the answer.

cases.answerText: **No.** The 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code limits the shutoff valve to 60 inches above the finished floor; it allows a higher valve only when the appliance’s gas connection is itself more than 60 inches high. With the connection at 40 inches, a valve at 62 inches exceeds the limit. (FGC § 409.5.1)

Since the connection is at 72 inches, the exception applies to the height limit; it does not waive the separate location and access requirements (FGC § 409.5.1).

cases.answerText: Ordinary underground gas piping must be at least **24 inches below grade**, measured to the **top of the pipe** (2022 NYC FGC § 404.12). The supplied exception allows less depth only with the specified steel protective plates; without that protection, the 24-inch minimum applies.

cases.label: correct_useful

cases.answerText: **No.** For a 4-inch outside-diameter pipe, a centerline 24 inches below grade puts the top of the pipe 22 inches below grade. The 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code requires the **top** of underground piping to be at least 24 inches below grade, so the centerline would need to be at least **26 inches** below grade. The stated depth does not meet that minimum without the specified steel-plate protection (FGC § 404.12).

cases.answerText: No. The 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code requires steel protective plates at least 1/4 inch thick for its reduced-burial-depth exception; a 1/8-inch plate is half that thickness and does not satisfy the specified minimum (FGC § 404.12).

The no-plate exception is needed only for burial shallower than 24 inches. (2022 NYC FGC § 404.12)

cases.answerText: **At least 18 inches (457 mm) below sprinkler head deflectors.** The 2022 NYC Fire Code sets that minimum for storage in areas protected by a sprinkler system; the stated exception concerns authorization for noncombustible materials near a fire partition, not ordinary storage (FC § 315.2.1).

cases.note: Storage clearance and measurement datum agree with FC315.2.1 and scenario arithmetic.
cases.answerText: **At least 2 feet (610 mm) below the ceiling** in a nonsprinklered building area (FC § 315.2.1). The department may authorize noncombustible materials to be stored to the ceiling when the storage is within 30 inches (762 mm) of a fire partition; absent that authorization, the 2-foot clearance applies.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Storage clearance and measurement datum agree with FC315.2.1 and scenario arithmetic.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** FC 315.2.1 requires storage in a sprinkler-protected area to be at least 18 inches below sprinkler deflectors. With the deflectors 2 inches below the ceiling and storage 20 inches below it, the clearance is 18 inches, meeting the minimum exactly (FC § 315.2.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correct16-inch calculation against18-inch deflector minimum.
cases.answerText: **No.** FC § 315.2.1 requires at least 18 inches below sprinkler-head deflectors. With the deflectors 2 inches below the ceiling and storage 18 inches below it, the clearance is 16 inches—2 inches short. Storage would need to be at least 20 inches below the ceiling to meet that minimum. The stated authorization for storage to the ceiling is limited to noncombustible materials within 30 inches of a fire partition and does not apply to this ordinary storage without special authorization.

cases.answerText:
**If it is a machinery room for a refrigerating system, no:** combustible materials may not be stored there, except for specified items such as spare parts, tools, and incidental materials necessary for safe system operation and maintenance (FC § 606.10). For a mechanical equipment room that is not such a refrigerating-system machinery room, the supplied evidence does not establish a general ban on cardboard boxes. Boxes also cannot be placed in the designated working space in front of electrical service equipment (FC § 605.3).

The room’s function determines whether the specific storage prohibition applies. Is it a refrigerating-system machinery room?

cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Fire Code, storage of noncombustible materials to the ceiling within 30 inches of a fire partition may be authorized by the department; being within 30 inches does not itself authorize ceiling-height storage. Without that authorization, the applicable ceiling-clearance rule remains: at least 2 feet below the ceiling in areas not protected by a sprinkler system, or at least 18 inches below sprinkler-head deflectors in sprinkler-protected areas (FC § 315.2.1).

cases.answerText: **Meeting the vertical-clearance requirement alone does not establish that storage may obstruct a means of egress.** The supplied 2022 NYC Building Code text defines an *accessible means of egress* as a “continuous and unobstructed way of egress travel,” but it does not provide the general rule governing storage obstructions or show that this definition resolves your situation (BC § 202). So I can’t determine from this evidence whether the storage is permitted.

cases.note: Authorization condition or bicycle count and rounding match source key.
cases.answerText: **6 enclosed bicycle spaces.** For residences other than single-family detached residences and affordable independent residences for seniors, ZR 25-811 requires 1 space per 2 dwelling units. For 11 units, 11 ÷ 2 = 5.5; because a fraction of 50% or greater counts as an additional space, the requirement is 6. The table’s waiver for buildings or building segments with 10 or fewer dwelling units does not apply to this 11-unit building. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Small-building waiver, per-building calculation and half-space rounding correctly retained across corrections.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** At exactly 10 dwelling units, the building falls within ZR 25-811’s waiver for bicycle-parking requirements accessory to buildings or building segments containing 10 dwelling units or less. The threshold includes 10, so the prior 11-unit result changes; this waives the stated bicycle-parking requirement, not other requirements. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Small-building waiver, per-building calculation and half-space rounding correctly retained across corrections.
cases.answerText: **At 12 dwelling units, the small-building waiver no longer applies.** Assuming the same ordinary residential use and a single building, ZR 25-811 requires 1 enclosed bicycle space per 2 dwelling units, so 12 units require **6 spaces**. The waiver covers buildings or building segments containing 10 dwelling units or less. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Small-building waiver, per-building calculation and half-space rounding correctly retained across corrections.
cases.answerText: At 13 dwelling units, the waiver for buildings or building segments containing 10 dwelling units or less does not apply. Assuming the same ordinary residential use and one building, the requirement is 1 enclosed bicycle space per 2 dwelling units; 13 ÷ 2 = 6.5, and a fraction of 50% or greater counts as an additional space, so **7 enclosed bicycle spaces** are required (ZR § 25-811).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Small-building waiver, per-building calculation and half-space rounding correctly retained across corrections.
cases.answerText: **No.** ZR 25-811 says the bicycle-parking requirement for residences is calculated separately for separate buildings or building segments, and waives the table requirement for spaces accessory to buildings or building segments containing 10 dwelling units or less. So two separate six-unit buildings are considered separately; each falls within the waiver, rather than combining to 12 units. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.answerText: **6 enclosed bicycle spaces.** ZR 25-811 treats 3 rooming units as 1 dwelling unit, so 33 rooming units equal 11 dwelling units. At 1 space per 2 dwelling units, that is 5.5 spaces; the rule counts a fraction of 50% or greater as an additional space, giving **6**. The waiver for buildings or building segments containing 10 dwelling units or less does not apply. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.label: correct_useful

cases.answerText: No. For the stated 33 rooming units, ZR 25-811 treats three rooming units as one dwelling unit, so the calculation is 33 ÷ 3 ÷ 2 = 5.5 spaces. It expressly counts a fraction of 50 percent or greater as an additional space, so the requirement is **6 spaces**, not 5. (ZR § 25-811)

cases.answerText: The default is **15 square feet per enclosed bicycle parking space**. ZR 25-83 permits reducing that area by up to 9 square feet per bicycle only if the Commissioner of Buildings certifies that the submitted layout adequately accommodates the specified number of bicycles; without that certified reduction, the default remains 15 square feet per space.

cases.answerText: **No.** ZR 25-83 requires 15 square feet per bicycle space; using 8 square feet would reduce that by 7 square feet per space, so it requires the Commissioner of Buildings’ certification that the submitted layout adequately accommodates the specified number of bicycles. Without certification, the 15-square-foot requirement applies.

cases.note: Rooming-unit conversion, rounding, certified area reduction or same-zoning-lot baseline matches source key.
cases.answerText: **6 square feet per enclosed bicycle parking space.** ZR 25-83 sets 15 square feet per space and permits a reduction of up to 9 square feet per bicycle when the Commissioner of Buildings certifies that the submitted layout adequately accommodates the specified number of bicycles: 15 − 9 = 6 square feet. (ZR § 25-83)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rooming-unit conversion, rounding, certified area reduction or same-zoning-lot baseline matches source key.
cases.answerText: No— ZR 25-83 allows a reduction of up to 9 square feet per bicycle from the 15-square-foot baseline only with the Commissioner of Buildings’ certification, so the maximum reduction yields **6 square feet per space** (15 − 9), not 5. A 5-square-foot space would require a 10-square-foot reduction, exceeding the stated maximum.

cases.answerText: The ordinary rule is that accessory bicycle parking spaces must be on the **same zoning lot** as the building or use they serve. The stated exception is ZR § 25-84, which allows qualifying required spaces off-site under its conditions; this answers the baseline location rule, not whether a particular off-site location qualifies. (ZR §§ 25-83, 25-84)

cases.answerText: **Yes, as to the distance criterion alone:** 900 feet is within ZR 25-84’s limit of not farther than 1,000 feet from the nearest boundary of the served zoning lot. That answers only the distance test; the off-site spaces must also satisfy the section’s other conditions, including its plaque and certificate-of-occupancy provisions. (ZR § 25-84)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Off-site distance and shared-subsurface alternative correctly applied without blanket approval.
cases.answerText: **At 1,100 feet, the ordinary off-site distance route does not qualify.** ZR § 25-84 permits off-site required bicycle spaces on another zoning lot only if it is no farther than 1,000 feet from the nearest boundary of the served lot, **or** the spaces are within a subsurface parking and other service facility serving multiple zoning lots, including the served lot. With no shared subsurface facility, neither stated route is met on these facts. The separate plaque and certificate-of-occupancy conditions do not cure that distance shortfall.
